title: Influence and copying: Lester Young, Armstrong's ripple, Bud Powell
summary: Gil says a sound becomes public property and recalls Lester Young mistaking a copy of himself on a jukebox.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Once you do something and play it, then it belongs in the wind.
But how do you feel when you hear yourself, well implicitly which is a matter of influence or explicitly which is sometimes a matter of fist....................(LAUGHTER).

It all depends on whether it's good or not. If it's good, okay. (LAUGHTER). If it's good you know. If it's not good it's a mess. You can't do anything about that. It's,you run into some big problems I think. Lester Young used to be so, they finally got so bad at it, he gave up his sound and style and everything because everybody else was doing it, right? It got to be so, I mean everybody playing every instrument was doing it. He influenced everybody really and especially those who play his tenor.

I remember one time we were, the juke box was playing right before we were ready to start playing. I was playing with him at an Army Camp and the record was playing and he said, gee, that's me! Oh, no that's not me.
Oh my goodness. Somebody had just copied him that closely.
Yes. And he thought all of a sudden it was him but all of a sudden he knew that it wasn't you know, but for a second he thought it was.
Now that is indeed explicit theft. (LAUGHTER). That you can steal somebody's tone.

Well it becomes part, it becomes public property you know. Once Louis Armstrong established his tone, it's like dropping a giant boulder into the sea and watching that thing go and ripple out you know. Everybody is affected by it you know. Music, all music is affected by it. Somebody who creates their own sound if it's beautiful and uses it in a tasteful way you know.
One hand it's flattery and on the other hand it's..........
Oh it's terrible if the person gets ripped off and doesn't get a chance to work himself you know. I remember one night when I first came
to New York I dashed up to (Bud Powell), I said, Bud, you're the end. He said, 'yes? give me a job!' (LAUGHTER). That took care of me, I said, well......
